readerTitle: Two cooks, same pay, very different futures
caseNote: 가상 사례 (두 요리사, 수셰프, 소프트웨어 개발자) + 개념 출처 (Cal Newport, 2012)
insight: 일과 자리를 오늘의 보수만이 아니라 그 일이 나에게 남기는 희소하고 가치 있는 자산으로 판단한다.
misconception: 경력은 연차와 직함이 쌓이면 저절로 커진다. 더 많이 주는 자리가 언제나 더 좋은 자리다.

sources.text: Newport, C. (2012). So Good They Can't Ignore You. Grand Central Publishing. ('career capital' 개념)
요리사·개발자 사례와 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Newport가 career capital을 '희소하고 가치 있는 기술'로 설명하고, 이를 더 나은 일과 자율성과 교환한다고 쓴 점을 원문으로 확인하세요. 카드에는 '희소하고 가치 있는 기술, 관계, 평판'으로 넓혀 풀어 썼습니다. 관계와 평판까지 포함한 것은 편집상의 확장입니다.
'같은 1년을 다섯 번 반복한다'는 표현은 널리 쓰이는 말로, 특정인의 인용으로 표시하지 않았습니다.
2번 카드의 시급 차이 $3는 설명용 가상 수치입니다.

cards.title: Two cooks, same pay, very different futures
body: Maya and Leo start at the same restaurant on the same day, for the same wage.
Five years later, one is asked to open the owner's second location. The other is still the fastest grill cook in town, and just as easy to replace as on day one.

image.label: Two cooks at a kitchen pass, one path branching wider
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 주방 패스 앞에 선 두 요리사. 한 명 발밑의 길은 계속 같은 그릴 앞을 맴돌고, 다른 한 명의 길은 여러 갈래(주문표, 메뉴판, 새 매장 문)로 넓어짐. 실제 브랜드나 로고 없음.

cards.title: Two job offers for a sous chef.
body: You're a sous chef. A busy chain offers you $3 more an hour to run the same station you run now. A smaller restaurant offers your current pay, but the chef will teach you menu costing and let you run the kitchen on Tuesdays.

options.text: The chain. More money now is a sure thing
options.feedback: You gain income you may truly need. But in two years you'll have the same skills, so your next raise depends on the same narrow job.

options.text: The smaller restaurant, for what you'll learn
options.feedback: You give up some pay now for skills few cooks have: costing a menu and running a shift. Those are what future employers pay for.

options.text: Stay put and ask for a raise
options.feedback: It feels safe and might get you a little more. But nothing about your work changes, so neither does your value.

cards.title: Leo got faster. Maya got rarer.
body: Back to our two cooks. Leo stayed on the grill. He got very fast, but speed on one station is a skill many cooks reach.

Maya said yes to the odd jobs: placing supplier orders, training new hires, costing a new dish. Each one was a little uncomfortable. Together they made her one of the few people who understood the whole kitchen. When the owner needed someone to open a new site, there was only one name on the list.

cards.title: Career capital
body: **Career capital** is the rare and valuable skills, relationships and reputation you build through your work.

Writer Cal Newport popularized the term in his 2012 book *So Good They Can't Ignore You*. His point: you trade this capital later for what you want, such as better roles, more pay or more freedom. You can't trade what you haven't built.

image.label: A savings jar filling with skills, contacts and reputation
image.brief: 유리 저금통 안에 동전 대신 "Skills", "Relationships", "Reputation" 라벨이 붙은 블록이 쌓임. 옆에 화살표로 "Better role", "More pay", "More freedom" 문으로 교환되는 모습. 플랫 일러스트.

cards.title: Not all experience counts the same.
body: Years on the job are not the same as capital. Some people gain five years of experience. Others repeat the same year five times. Capital grows when your work is:
list: **Rare:** few people around you can do it
**Valuable:** someone would pay for it or depends on it
**Visible:** others can see the results you produced
cards.callout: A task that stretches you and that others notice is usually worth more than a raise of the same size.
cards.softwareNote: In software, maintaining a tool nobody else touches is comfortable but invisible. Owning a risky migration that the whole company relies on builds skill and reputation at the same time.

cards.title: Owners and managers build it too.
body: A café owner's capital is a loyal supplier who calls first when prices drop, and a name that lets new menu items sell on trust.

Managers shape their team's capital every time they hand out work. The person who always gets the routine jobs falls behind. Spreading the stretch assignments is one of the cheapest ways to grow people and keep them.

cards.title: Hard is not the same as valuable.
body: Capital only counts if someone else values it. Mastering a dish no one orders, or a system your industry is leaving, is effort without return.
Money today matters too. If rent is due, the higher-paying job can be the right call. And capital has to be spent. If you never ask for the bigger role, you just have a full jar.

cards.title: Now you're a software developer.
body: Your manager offers you a choice of next project. Which builds the most career capital?

options.text: Keep maintaining the internal tool you know inside out
options.feedback: Low stress and you'll look reliable. But you learn little new, and few people outside your team see the work.

options.text: Join the senior team moving the payment system to a new platform
options.feedback: It's harder and riskier, but you learn a rare skill from strong people on work the whole company notices.

options.text: Spend the quarter learning a trendy framework no team here uses
options.feedback: You may gain a skill, but nobody here needs it yet, so it adds little to your reputation or options right now.

cards.title: Judge work by what it leaves you with.
body: Pay is what a job gives you today. Career capital is what it leaves you with: rare skills, people who trust you and a reputation others can see.
**Try it today:** list the three tasks you did most this week. Next to each, write one thing it taught you that few people around you can do. Where the line is blank, look for a stretch task.
